doc.title: John Budd interviewed by Monk Rowe, Aspen, Colorado, October 11, 1997 [transcript only]

title: Awe at musicians; musicians and doctors admire each other's professions
summary: Rowe and Budd compare admiration across trades, and Budd on medicine postponing death and caring for the patient.

story.theme_name: Late-career reflections: awards, legacy and life lessons
story.community_name: Looking back: no regrets, what it all meant

blocks.x: I think it’s so neat because it’s almost like if you were living in Beethoven’s time being able to actually hear Beethoven play.

But we have our Beethovens. We have our masters of this kind of music and so many of them have passed on but there’s still a decent amount that are still here. And to be able to hear them, it’s a great luxury.

But I’ll take more of your time. I could talk for days. It’s not that I’m just trying to tell someone how much I know or anything like that, I’m just in awe of these people, that they know me, and they’re good to me, and I think I can play the piano fairly well but not in their league at all. And I say it’s about the same thing as if a carpenter took out your appendix, it’s pretty good.
Yeah but you know I think most musicians, even the top guys, they look at other professions and they say the same thing.
I mean how can you operate on people? How can you possibly do that? And I think of a plumber who comes to my house and fixes things that I couldn’t even begin to know even what tools to have.

I’m glad to hear you say that because I feel that way too. And the marvelous things they do. And I say we have an edge in medicine I tell them all. Because half the things that people get wrong, will get well if you do nothing. Because life is meant to be well and spontaneous healing occurs in half the things. Of course they come to a doctor for assurance, for symphomatic relief, you can relieve pain, you can relieve sleeplessness, you can increase appetite. But you don’t save lives. One of my friends used to say we don’t save lives, we postpone death. Because life is a fatal disease eventually. And somebody said maybe it’s better that you die now of that car accident then to live and die of Alzheimer’s disease or something like that. There are choices that you can’t make, but life is good to you in so many ways. But what you save in repairing things, anything an engineer or a carpenter or a bricklayer does, it’s got to be done. fix it. A sick person, you’re going to do the best you can but he may not make it, or maybe you’ll find some magic, but that’s exceptional I think. I’m not putting down medicine because the important thing is caring for the patient, not the disease. One of my teacher said don’t forget that patient care means caring for the patient. And that’s not just — it’s a good word.
